'''''Lucuma bifera''''' (synonym ''Pouteria lucuma'') is a species of [[tree]] in the family [[Sapotaceae]], cultivated for its fruit, the '''lúcuma'''. It is native to the [[Andes|Andean]] valleys of [[Colombia]], [[Ecuador]], [[Peru]], [[Bolivia]], and northern [[Chile]].<ref name = powo/><ref name=capitulo1>{{cite web|url=http://www.biblioteca.udep.edu.pe/bibvirudep/tesis/pdf/1_161_186_112_1548.pdf|title=CAPÍTULO I: LA LÚCUMA (in Spanish)|publisher=University of Piura, Peru}}</ref><ref name="morton">{{cite web|url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/lucmo.html|title=Lucmo|author=Morton JF|date=1987|publisher=Purdue University, republished from p. 405–406. In: Fruits of Warm Climates. Julia F. Morton, Miami, FL}}</ref>

== Description ==
This evergreen tree is up to {{Convert|20|m|abbr=on}} tall, and has greyish-brown, fissured bark, which produces a milky white exudate.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=Flora Neotropica Monograph Sapotaceae|last=Pennington|first=T. D.|date=1990|publisher=New York Botanical Garden|isbn=9780893273446|pages=383–385|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite book|title=Exotic Fruits and Nuts of the New World|last1=Duarte|first1=Odilo|last2=Paull|first2=Robert|date=2015|publisher=CABI|isbn=9781780645056|pages=117–123|language=en}}</ref> The end of branchlets and the petioles are covered with short, brown hairs.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> The leaves are simple, oblanceolate to elliptical, up to {{Convert|25|cm|abbr=on}} long and {{Convert|10|cm|abbr=on}} wide, and [[Glossary of botanical terms#G|glabrous]] (or sometimes slightly hairy on the underside) grouped at the end of the branches.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Flowers are solitary or in [[Fascicle (botany)|fascicles]], small, [[Axillary bud|axillary]], with hairy [[sepal]]s and a [[Petal|corolla]] forming a tube {{Convert|1.0-1.8|cm|abbr=on}} long, greenish white, with five lobes, five stamens, five [[staminode]]s, a pubescent ovary, and a [[Stigma (botany)#Style|style]] {{Convert|0.8-1.5|cm|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> The fruit is [[wiktionary:globose|globose]], {{Convert|6-12|cm|abbr=on}} long, [[Glabrousness|glabrous]], and russet to yellow when mature; the pulp is bright yellow; the one to several seeds are {{Convert|1.8-3.5|cm|abbr=on}} long, dark brown, and glossy.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />[[File:Lúcuma.png|left|thumb|197x197px|Lucumas.]]

==History==
Representations of lúcuma have been found on ceramics at burial sites of the indigenous people of coastal Peru.<ref name="morton" /> The [[Moche culture|Moche]] people had a fascination with agriculture and often chose to represent fruits and vegetables, including lúcuma, in their art.<ref>Berrin, Katherine & Larco Museum. ''The Spirit of Ancient Peru:Treasures from the [[Larco Museum|Museo Arqueológico Rafael Larco Herrera]].'' New York: [[Thames and Hudson]], 1997.</ref>

The fruit was first seen and reported by Europeans in Ecuador in 1531.<ref name="morton" /><ref>''Lesser-known and under-utilised plant resources'' Ameenah Gurib-Fakim - 2005 - Page 59</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
The area of origin of ''L. bifera'' is located in the Andes of Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, and northern Chile,<ref name=powo/> at temperate elevations of {{convert|2700-3000|m|ft|abbr=on}}.<ref name="morton" />

==Cultivation==
[[File:Lucumalarcomuseum.jpg|left|thumb|[[Moche culture]] pottery representing lucumas.]]In addition to Peru, the fruit is grown also to a limited extent in [[Bolivia]], [[Chile]] and [[Costa Rica]].  Attempts at growing lúcuma in Florida's climate are typically not successful.<ref name="morton" /> The fruit is successfully grown in [[Vietnam]], where it is known as lêkima.

In Peru, harvesting season is from October to March and in Chile from June to November.<ref name="capitulo1" />

==Uses==
When eaten raw, the very sweet fruit is bright yellow and has a mealy and dry texture.<ref name="morton" /> In Peru, it is more commonly used as a flavor in juice, [[milkshake]]s, and especially [[ice cream]]. Its flavor in such preparations has been described variously as being similar to [[sweet potato]], [[maple syrup]], or [[butterscotch]]. In Peru, {{lang|es|manjar de lúcuma}} ({{lang|es|[[dulce de leche]]}} with lúcuma purée) is a [[dessert]]. Multiple sources describe it as the most popular ice cream flavor in Peru<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.limaeasy.com/peruvian-food-guide/typical-peruvian-fruits/lucuma|title=Lucuma}}</ref> and one of the most popular fresh fruits.

==Nutrition==
Lúcuma pulp has a 64–72% [[water content|moisture content]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |title=The Encyclopedia of Fruit and Nuts |last1=Janick |first1=Jules |last2=Paull |first2=Robert E. |date=2008 |publisher=CABI |isbn=9780851996387 |pages=837 |language=en }}</ref> The pulp also contains [[glucose]], [[fructose]], [[sucrose]], [[inositol]], [[citric acid]], and [[succinic acid]].<ref name=":0" />
